anchors.fact: He liked to tell people a shark had eaten his leg (Difford's, Sutcliffe, secondary; F7), and as his fame grew many believed it (Beyl 2015, secondary; F8).
anchors.meaning: The hard thing, told as an adventure, and people leaned in. His telling rests on one page: "he liked to tell people", never "always" or "everyone".
anchors.speaksTo: they tell their struggles as adventures so the struggle doesn't win

anchors.fact: He lost a leg as a boy (Oxford pdf 258; Beyl; Difford's; F2). No cause, no age (C1, C2).
anchors.meaning: Said once, plainly. The mirror is the telling, never the loss.

anchors.fact: After leaving school, a run of jobs that didn't last, selling paint and tyres among other things; then in 1934 a barbecue shack in Oakland, Hinky Dink's, where he was owner, bartender and cook (Oxford pdf 258; F3–F4). He opened it with $800 borrowed from an aunt, and at first it held about thirty workers from the neighbourhood (Beyl; F4).
anchors.meaning: The life without the shark was already worth telling.
anchors.speaksTo: a plain life, told plainly, that nobody remembers

anchors.fact: "Trader" came from his habit of trading meals for goods and services, and he renamed the shack Trader Vic's (Beyl, secondary, single source; F6).
anchors.meaning: The big name grew from a plain habit, and the plain root is the better tale. Never "the Trader was a fake".
anchors.speaksTo: make life larger in the telling

anchors.fact: In later years, sitting with a special customer, he liked to pull the artificial leg out from under the table and tell them not to get one unless they really needed it (Beyl; F9).
anchors.meaning: The same man could tell it plainly, with a joke in it, and it still held the table. Touches the leg itself: Wren decides if it's safe for a reader who has lost a limb.

anchors.fact: In 1938 the shack became Trader Vic's; by his death in 1984 there were more than twenty, across North America, Europe and Japan, and his bar guide is still counted a classic of its kind (Oxford pdf 258; F12).
anchors.meaning: The legend was never the whole person.

anchors.fact: His Mai Tai, as he told it: 1944, the service bar of his Oakland restaurant, aged Jamaican rum, fresh lime, orange curaçao, rock candy syrup and almond orgeat, shaken hard with shaved ice, half the lime shell and a branch of mint; he gave two to friends from Tahiti, and the name came from what Carrie Guild said (*Joy* pdf 327; Oxford pdf 1210–1211; F13–F14). A rival's 1933 Mai Tai tasted almost nothing like it, and it was Vic's formula that rose (Oxford pdf 1211; F15).
anchors.meaning: The one thing he made that everyone still knows: "his Mai Tai", "the drink he said he created". Never "he invented the Mai Tai" flat.

anchors.fact: By 1955 the name had spread through the islands while his recipe stayed a secret, so rivals mixed rum and juice under it; by the 1970s the only place making it properly was Trader Vic's (Oxford pdf 1211–1212; F16).
anchors.kind: provenance (the epigraph only; y4's sentence cut, Hester r4)
anchors.meaning: The name travelled; the real thing underneath was better. Provenance only, never a second reveal.
anchors.speaksTo: the real thing doing the work underneath

anchors.fact: Our orgeat is made at home from almonds toasted first; the *Flavor Matrix* says nuts should be toasted to bring out their flavour (pdf 184). Vic's own orgeat was a bought French one, "for its subtle almond flavor" (*Joy* pdf 327; F18). Before the Trader, he was owner, bartender and cook of the shack, and drew on his cooking skills for his drinks (Oxford pdf 258; F4, F11).
anchors.meaning: The cook's step from the plain record, signposted as our reading ("I like to think…"). Never "he toasted his almonds" or "his orgeat".
anchors.speaksTo: the real thing doing the work underneath

anchors.fact: Appleton Estate became part of J. Wray and Nephew Ltd. in the early twentieth century (Oxford pdf 132; F19); the firm runs more than one distillery (pdf 1698), and Vic's seventeen-year Wray & Nephew is long defunct (pdf 1212).
anchors.meaning: From the firm whose name was on his bottle; never "the same rum" or "the same distillery".

cocktail.closingLine: Take the almonds to gold before anything else: that's where the taste is.
cocktail.glassware: double old-fashioned glass (about 350 ml), packed with crushed ice
method: Make the almond syrup a day ahead, or that morning. Spread 150 g blanched almonds on a baking tray and toast them in the oven at 180°C for 8 to 10 minutes, until pale gold and smelling toasted. Let them cool. Blend them with 300 ml cold water for a minute, leave it 30 minutes, then squeeze it all through a clean cloth into a bowl. Weigh the almond milk, pour it into a pan with the same weight of white sugar, and warm it gently, stirring, until the sugar has gone (don't let it boil). Off the heat, stir in ¼ teaspoon orange flower water. Bottle it: about 400 ml, two weeks in the fridge.
Make crushed ice: wrap a tray of ice cubes in a clean tea towel and bash it with a rolling pin.
Squeeze the lime, measure 30 ml of juice, and keep half the shell.
Put the rum, lime, curaçao, almond syrup and sugar syrup in a shaker with a big scoop of the crushed ice. Shake hard for about ten seconds.
Pour everything, ice and all, into the glass. Pack more crushed ice on top until it mounds over the rim.
Push the half lime shell into the ice, cut side up. Squeeze the mint branch once in your hand so it smells, and stand it up beside the shell.
cocktail.name: Hold the Shark

recipe.item: Appleton Estate 12 Year Old Rare Casks Jamaica rum (43%), recommended, or any aged Jamaican rum, the oldest you can find
recipe.note: Vic's seventeen-year Wray & Nephew is long gone. Appleton Estate became part of J. Wray and Nephew, the firm behind Vic's rum, in the early twentieth century.

recipe.item: fresh lime juice (about one lime; keep half the shell)
recipe.note: measure it: a big lime's juice pushes the drink too sharp

recipe.item: toasted almond orgeat (an almond syrup scented with orange flower water), made at home (method, step 1)
recipe.note: the almonds go in the oven first, like anything a cook wants to taste of more

recipe.item: big branch of fresh mint, standing up out of the ice
the squeezed lime shell, dropped in

cocktail.tagline: Your worst days become everyone's favourite stories.

reading.epigraph: Its name went round the islands long before its recipe did.
whoYouAre: A flat tyre on the motorway, in the rain, with no signal. By Friday it's the best thing anybody's heard all month: there's a tow-truck driver who sang the whole way, a hailstone the size of a plum, and a lorry that people ask you to do again. All of it happened, more or less. You simply know which version deserves to be the one people keep.

What nobody at the table knows is that the bigger the story, the worse it really was. The forty minutes on the hard shoulder, cold, and sure nobody was coming, never make it in. Told plainly, a bad day might sound like weakness. Worse, it might sound like nothing much, and be forgotten by the weekend. So you tell it larger, until the bad day is the small thing in it. The people listening go home believing their own bad week will pass, and might even be funny one day. That's a real kindness, and it's why they keep asking for another.
yours: Victor Bergeron lost a leg as a boy. Years later, when people knew him as Trader Vic, the man behind a chain of South Seas restaurants and the Mai Tai most people know, he liked to tell them that a shark had eaten it. As he got famous, plenty believed it. Maybe a shark really did. The odds are against it.

The plain version goes like this. He left school, then tried one job after another, selling paint and tyres among other things, and none of them lasted. (Yes, tyres. I didn't make that bit up.) In 1934, in his early thirties, he opened a barbecue shack in Oakland with $800 borrowed from an aunt, and ran it as owner, bartender and cook. One writer says that's where the nickname began, with his habit of trading meals for goods and services. Four years later the shack became Trader Vic's, and by the time he died there were more than twenty, across North America, Europe and Japan.

I like to think he knew the shark was the better line at a table. But look at the plain version again: the jobs that didn't last, the borrowed money, a cook paying his way in meals, and a name that grew out of it. None of it needs a shark. It's a terrific story as it stands, and it was his all along. So is your own. The version you tell is a gift, and it does people good. The one you leave out would hold the table just as well.

The cocktail I've made for you is his Mai Tai, the renowned classic. I built it on his own account of making it, which he dated to 1944: aged Jamaican rum, fresh lime, almond syrup, orange curaçao, a dash of sugar syrup, all shaken hard with shaved ice, then half the squeezed lime shell and a branch of fresh mint standing up out of the glass. This one keeps close to his formula, and the main change is mine. He used a French almond syrup. I make mine at home and toast the almonds to pale gold first, the way a cook would, as a nod to the cook he was before anyone called him Trader. I like to think the cook in him would have approved. It's golden and cold, sharp with lime first, then round and nutty underneath.

So keep telling them. The shark stays: people need it, and you're good at it. But once, tell one exactly as big as it was. I'd bet the table goes just as quiet. And what they'll remember afterwards won't be the shark. It'll be you.
